sentences.text: The name Asiatosuchus translates to "Asian crocodile".
Species within this genus display a generalized crocodilian form, featuring flat skulls that appear triangular when viewed from above.
Their upper jaw teeth completely overlapped the lower jaw teeth, creating a distinct overbite.
Based on largely complete skeletons, Asiatosuchus may have grown up to 4 meters long.
A. germanicus is estimated to have reached a length of 6.5 meters.
The type species A. grangeri was named by paleontologist Charles Mook in 1940.
Mook also established the genus Asiatosuchus in that same year.
Well-preserved remains from Germany and France were described in 1966 and assigned to the new species A. germanicus.
A. depressifrons was first named in 1855 under the name Crocodilus depressifrons.
This species is distinguishable from others by features including a large hole and depression in the jugal bone.
In 1964, Chinese paleontologist Yang Zhongjian named A. nanlingensis based on fragmentary material from the Shanghu Formation in Guangdong, China.
Two species were named from Russia: A. zajsanicus in 1982 and A. volgensis in 1993.
Small fossilized coprolites, or feces, were found alongside the specimen of A. nanlingensis.
The presence of a possible Asiatosuchus specimen in marine deposits suggests these crocodilians could tolerate prolonged time in the ocean.
This tolerance for marine environments may have aided the spread of early crocodilians across Europe and Asia.
Phylogenetic analyses classify Asiatosuchus as a member of the evolutionary group Crocodyloidea.
Recent analyses place Asiatosuchus as a basal member of Crocodyloidea, near the evolutionary split from Alligatoroidea.
The genus is classified within the parent group Crocodyloidea.
A 2021 morphological study determined that A. nanlingensis is the sister taxon of Kambara murgonensis within the subfamily Mekosuchinae.
The fossil range of Asiatosuchus spans from the Paleocene to the Eocene.
The genus lived from the Selandian to the Priabonian stages, between 60.9 and 33.9 million years ago.
Asiatosuchus is an extinct genus of crocodyloid that inhabited Eurasia during the Paleogene.
The German remains of A. germanicus came from the Messel Pit quarry, a site preserving life from Eocene anoxic lakes and subtropical forests.
These German fossils originated from the Messel fossil site, where anoxic lakes preserved various forms of life.
A Pakistani fossil was found in the Middle Eocene Drazinda Formation, a marine deposit that also preserved archaeocete whale remains.
Recent studies suggest that only the species A. grangeri belongs in the genus Asiatosuchus.
It is debated whether A. nanlingensis and Eoalligator chunyii are synonymous, though some researchers agree they are the same species.

A 2016 analysis proposed that A. nanlingensis and Eoalligator chunyii were synonyms, but a 2017 article disputed this, treating them as distinct species and suggesting the genus Asiatosuchus is paraphyletic.
A. volgensis and A. zajsanicus were regarded as nomina dubia because they are based on specimens with very little preserved anatomical detail.
Several species tend to be interpreted as nomina dubia because their type specimens lack sufficient unique anatomical characteristics for classification as different species.
In 1998, Angielczyk and Gingerich considered A. volgensis and A. zajsanicus to be nomina dubia due to poor preservation of the fossils.
